---
title: "Check & process your tracks"
description: "Inspect data quality, drop bad points, fill gaps, and smooth trajectories — all within the aniframe."
order: 4
---

Raw tracking data is rarely clean: trackers lose sight of keypoints, mislabel
points with high confidence, and jitter frame-to-frame. Before you compute a
single metric, it pays to **check** what you have and **process** it into shape.
Two packages handle this:
[anicheck](https://animovement.dev/anicheck) diagnoses quality, and
[aniprocess](https://animovement.dev/aniprocess) fixes it — both operating on the
same [aniframe](movement-data.qmd) you read in.

We'll pick up right where [Read your data](read-data.qmd) left off:

```r
library(animovement)

movement <- read_deeplabcut(get_sample_data("deeplabcut"))
```

## 1. Check data quality {#sec-check}

[anicheck](https://animovement.dev/anicheck) gives you three diagnostics.
They summarise a problem without changing your data, so you can decide how
aggressively to clean.

```r
# How confident was the tracker, per keypoint?
movement |> check_confidence()

# How big are the gaps of missing values?
movement |> check_na_gapsize()

# When in the recording do missing values occur?
movement |> check_na_timing()
```

Each returns a small summary table. Pair it with
[anivis](https://animovement.dev/anivis) to *see* the distribution — calling
`plot()` on a check result draws it:

```r
movement |> check_confidence() |> plot()
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Why check confidence first?
Pose-estimation exports often contain low-confidence points that still read as
perfectly valid coordinates. If you don't screen them out, those outliers
propagate into every downstream speed, distance and angle. Always look at
confidence before processing.
:::

## 2. Drop low-confidence points {#sec-drop}

`filter_na_confidence()` replaces the coordinates of any point below a
confidence threshold with `NA` — turning "the tracker guessed here" into an
honest gap you can deal with next:

```r
movement <- movement |>
  filter_na_confidence(threshold = 0.6)
```

*aniprocess* has a family of `filter_na_*()` functions for this — for example,
`filter_na_range()` (values outside a plausible range),
`filter_na_roi()` (outside a region of interest) and
`filter_na_speed()` (physically impossible jumps).

## 3. Fill the gaps {#sec-interpolate}

Now interpolate across those `NA`s. `replace_na_linear()` fills a gap by drawing
a straight line between the known points on either side. The `max_gap` argument
is your safety valve — leave long gaps unfilled rather than inventing data
across them:

```r
movement <- movement |>
  dplyr::group_by(individual, keypoint) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    x = replace_na_linear(x, max_gap = 5),
    y = replace_na_linear(y, max_gap = 5)
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()
```

We group by `individual` and `keypoint` so interpolation never bleeds from one
track into another. Prefer a smoother fill? Swap in `replace_na_spline()`, or
carry the last value forward with `replace_na_locf()`.

## 4. Smooth the trajectory {#sec-smooth}

Finally, tame frame-to-frame jitter. `filter_rollmedian()` applies a rolling
median — great for removing spikes while keeping edges crisp:

```r
movement <- movement |>
  dplyr::group_by(individual, keypoint) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    x = filter_rollmedian(x, window_width = 5),
    y = filter_rollmedian(y, window_width = 5)
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()
```

For a gentler, weighted smooth, reach for `filter_gaussian()` or
`filter_sgolay()` (Savitzky–Golay); for model-based smoothing of noisy tracks,
`filter_kalman()`.

## Putting it together {#sec-together}

The whole clean-up reads as one pipe:

```r
clean <- read_deeplabcut(get_sample_data("deeplabcut")) |>
  filter_na_confidence(threshold = 0.6) |>
  dplyr::group_by(individual, keypoint) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    x = replace_na_linear(x, max_gap = 5),
    y = replace_na_linear(y, max_gap = 5),
    x = filter_rollmedian(x, window_width = 5),
    y = filter_rollmedian(y, window_width = 5)
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()
```

You still have an aniframe — same structure you started with, just cleaner.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Keep going
Your data is analysis-ready. From here you can compute metrics with
[animetric](https://animovement.dev/animetric) — for example,
`calculate_kinematics()` adds speed, heading and acceleration — and plot the
result with [anivis](https://animovement.dev/anivis)' `plot_trajectory()`. See
both in a full, cross-package walkthrough in the
[tutorials](../learn/index.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## A note on reproducibility
Code blocks in these guides are shown for reference and aren't executed when the
site is built. Run them in your own R session — starting from
`get_sample_data()` — to reproduce every step against the latest package
versions.
:::
